title: Pennsylvania Study Abroad Experience
paragraphs: I am 加藤千尋, who took part in the Heisei 29 fiscal year overseas exchange program. First of all, I would like to express my deep gratitude for the great support I received before departure for this exchange program from Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 of the International Collaboration Office, who gave me advice many times, Ms. 西尾 of the exchange student section, Dr. 田中, the representative organizer of the Frontier Association, and Dr. 三井 of the Department of Tumor Pathology and Molecular Pathology, who wrote my letter of recommendation. In addition, many Frontier Association alumni doctors gave fruitful lectures at the Saturday classes before departure, and at my destinations I was greatly helped by Dr. 西崎 of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, Dr. 兼井 of Beth Israel Medical Center, Dr. 高山 of Columbia University, and Dr. 吉見 of Freiburg University. I would like to take this opportunity to thank them.

From 2/28 to 3/24 I was at the PICU division of the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, affiliated with the University of Pennsylvania, in the United States; during my stay in New York from 3/25 to 3/29 I was allowed to observe cardiology at Beth Israel and cardiology at Columbia University; and from 4/4 to 4/7 I observed hematology at the children's hospital of Freiburg University in Germany. In expressing my thanks, I once again feel how many people's support made this study abroad possible.

The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, CHOP, where I spent four weeks, has the longest history among children's hospitals in the United States and is an excellent hospital in both name and reality, constantly ranked near the top in American children's hospital rankings. I spent four weeks there in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit, PICU. My days were attending the resident lecture that began shortly after 7 every morning, the general rounds from 9 to 12, the one-hour Noon conference while eating lunch, resolving the day's questions before the 4 o'clock going-home time, and writing a report after getting home. My impression is that almost everything was hard and I was fully occupied just getting through each day, but looking back, I think there are also a few things I was able to achieve in the four weeks. What I keenly felt right after the clerkship started was that my advance study of ICU management was insufficient. More than the language barrier, the barrier of medical knowledge loomed large, and it was extremely difficult to hear and understand the exchanges between the senior doctors and residents on the daily rounds, which should have been the greatest fruit, and I was often at a loss as to what I should learn here and take home. However, of course I did not spend the month without any growth, and the daily correction of my reports by Dr. 西崎, who made my observership at CHOP possible, was the hardest and, I felt, the most training of all the study I have done in English. In order to write a report every day, I had the motivation during the day to learn something new, and rather than just writing down the knowledge I heard, I searched for the papers behind that knowledge and put it into sentences, replacing it with my own words as much as possible. This series of work is fundamental to studying anything, not only medicine, but it is something that tends to be neglected. As long as we have access, we can read papers from all over the world on the smartphone in our hands, so I felt to the bone that the depth and solidity of knowledge depend entirely on each person's diligence. When I realized that texts written in Japanese are only a small part of the texts written in English, it was a shock to me, who had until now studied medicine only within them. Understanding English "quickly" and "accurately," at least in reading, is a basic premise, and I felt the need for English literacy on my skin.

In the ICU during the day I witnessed many scenes I had never experienced, such as rounds with the family, over 20 staff responding to an emergency without confusion, the attitude of doctors at the time of death, then explanations about organ transplantation, and debriefing by all the staff after seeing a patient through to the end. It is true that there were many frustrating scenes in which I thought I could have made it more my own if I had been more capable, but I think it will be an experience that lashes my complacency and spurs me on in the future.

The morning resident lecture and the MOCK CODE (pediatric emergency call) simulation held every Thursday were occasions where I could taste the sense of accomplishment of managing to keep up and understand. Learning with simulation is also a field in which Dr. 西崎 has long been involved. It was an interesting experience to look from above at the stumbling and difficulty when several people with different strengths treat a patient. A doctor must bear the responsibility, in an emergency, of being a leader who assigns work appropriately to the available staff and gives instructions to save the patient's life by the shortest route. I shrank a little at the weight of the duty, but it was also an experience that made me want to steel myself.

The day after finishing my stay in Philadelphia, I moved to New York. It was so stimulating that it was hard to believe it was a short stay of three and a half days. I was allowed to observe cardiology at Beth Israel Medical Center, where Dr. 兼井, who also instructed us at the pre-departure study session, works. Since it is a so-called community hospital, it had a different feel from CHOP and many patients were admitted and discharged. In the afternoon I followed him to the office with the outpatient clinic and observed his clinic. In fact, I was very surprised to learn at the dinner to which he invited me that on this day he had done an emergency cath from 4 in the morning and, in a schedule of two scheduled caths, rounds, outpatient clinic, and study for the specialist examination in the evening, had made time for me. At Beth Israel there is a glass-walled passageway from which the skyscrapers of Manhattan spread across the entire field of view. Dr. 兼井, who told me it is a favorite place where he can feel the energy of this city, was simply cool. The next day, through the kindness of Dr. 高山 of Columbia University in the northwest of Manhattan Island, to whom Dr. 兼井 introduced me, I was allowed to observe cardiac surgery for a day. It was an amazing environment in which most of the doctors on the cardiac surgery staff at Columbia University were Japanese. These days it is said, with an air of truth, that the Japanese are being pushed aside by other Asian countries, but it was a truly wonderful experience to see my seniors, who have firmly taken root in New York, the center of the world, and are spoken of with trust by other staff and patients.

Finally, relying on Dr. 吉見 of the hematology department of the children's hospital of Freiburg University, to whom I was introduced by Dr. 田中, the representative organizer of the Frontier Association, I flew to Germany. Freiburg is a city in southwestern Germany near Switzerland. I was stunned that the medical staff's conversations were in German to a degree beyond my expectations, but by this time I was able to get along with a considerably sturdier heart. I followed the rounds, being attended to in English by the students who were rotating, and receiving comments from the supervising doctors, and in spare moments Dr. 吉見 taught me how to read blood smears. The evening before leaving Freiburg, I was invited to dinner by Dr. 吉見 and listened to his stories. Here too, touching the resilience of a doctor working in a land far from Japan made my heart burn. It is an aside, but if you go to Freiburg in spring in future years, please do eat white asparagus. It will change your concept of asparagus.

Starting with a sudden advancing, change and addition of procedures for my destination, and with the busy schedule of attending Clinical Clerkship I until the day before leaving for the United States and Clinical Clerkship II immediately after returning to Japan, looking back, from the preparation stage of the study abroad the days were more stimulating than any I have had. There were times when it was difficult to find meaning in going abroad, amid various hesitations and unexpected events, but with the support of people in Japan and abroad, now that the study abroad has ended I am very grateful to have been allowed to go. My greatest asset is that I was able to see with my own eyes, and hear directly the stories of, the seniors and Japanese doctors of Nagoya University working and doing well every day, in Japan of course but also somewhere in the world. The doctors' stories, heard in the heightened state of mind that being overseas brings, remain in my heart more strongly than usual, and I feel they have become a support for my heart. In some countries, the United States being one example, it seems that accepting students is becoming more difficult year by year. I feel I was very fortunate to be given this opportunity through the efforts of the professors. I too want to become a person who can make efforts for those who come after. Finally, I would like to close my return report by wishing for the continued development of the Frontier Association.
